scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Gombey originated among Bermuda's enslaved population, drawing from African, Caribbean, and Indigenous influences.
Genetic studies of Black Bermudians show ancestry linked to a band across southern Africa from Angola to Mozambique, distinct from other British West Indian populations.
Historically, the dance was a form of protest; masked performers used the anonymity of the costume to mock slave masters.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally a tool of resistance and a rare outlet for celebration under slavery, the Gombey is now performed at major national holidays and community events.
It is a staple of Boxing Day, New Year's Day, and Bermuda Day.
It also appears at football and cricket matches.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed as a procession or a series of ritualized face-offs.
The Lead Indian or Bowman scouts ahead with a bow and arrow, while Warriors carry tomahawks on their shoulders.
A signature element is the 'cockfight,' where two dancers face off in a display of agility and mock combat.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is purely percussive and rhythmic, led by the 'Mother' drum (bass) and accompanied by at least two snare drums and a kettle drum.
The snare drummers play intricate riffs and call-and-response patterns over the Mother drum's steady pulse.
Listen for the Mother drum (bass), Snare drum, Kettle drum, Fife.

A dense percussive soundscape dominated by the sharp, military-style snapping of snare drums playing complex syncopations against a deep, steady bass drum pulse. Whistles pierce the rhythm to signal changes, creating a high-energy, driving atmosphere.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Gombey costumes provide full-body coverage and are highly decorative.
Key features include tall headdresses topped with peacock feathers, painted masks, and long capes.
The outfits are adorned with tassels, mirrors, and bells that create sound as the dancer moves.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The tradition is led by Captains who oversee individual troupes and determine their unique styles.
Historically, individuals like Ajax and Mentor are recorded as participants in the 1831 'Gumba' procession.
While the Gombey is specific to Bermuda, it shares roots with the Bahamian Goombay and shows similarities to Mummers and Morris dancing.
The Gombey lineage includes African rhythmic traditions (specifically from the Angola-Mozambique corridor), Caribbean masquerade, and Indigenous North American war dances (Wampanoag and Pequot).

images.description: Gombey dancers performing in Kings Square,St. George's, Bermuda.

The Gombey is an iconic symbol of Bermuda, this folklife tradition reflecting the island’s blend of African, Caribbean and British cultures, incorporating them over time into a unique performance art full of colorful and intricate masquerade, dance and drumming.
Hamilton, Pembroke Parish, Bermudas.
